$comment: Rules about the reasoning errors that a document reproduces rather than corrects: extrapolating the recent past, reading a return table as a forecast, and reaching a conclusion nothing could overturn. Standard 24.
$admissionTest: Standard 24 R2 — that price movement must not be offered as a reason — is deliberately given no id here. It is already carried by the forbidden-level `prohibited.price-momentum-recommendation`, and a second id asking the same question would raise `frameworkCoverage` without checking anything more. R5 is kept out entirely: the responses it recommends depend on personal circumstances outside the document, so its violation cannot be explained with information the framework has, and no evidence in the artifact distinguishes an author who considered them from one who did not.

rules.title: A historical rate states the period it was measured over and why that period is representative
rules.description: Where a document uses a historical return as a forward assumption, it states the window the figure was measured over and argues that the window is representative of the horizon being projected.
rules.rationale: Recent performance is the weakest available predictor and the most psychologically available one. The measurement window is where the extrapolation hides: a rate taken from a decade-long bull market and a genuine long-run estimate look identical on the page once the window is omitted.
rules.remediation: State the sample period beside the rate, say why it is representative of the horizon being projected, and vary the rate across scenarios rather than carrying one figure forward.
rules.$assuranceNote: Lexical: it establishes that a period and a justification are PRESENT, never that the justification is SOUND or the period representative. Whether a stated forward rate was in fact lifted from recent performance is not evaluable from a document at all, because the provenance of an assumption is exactly what the failure omits — which is why Standard 12 keeps the wider question in prose.

rules.title: A historical series carries a non-predictiveness qualification at the point of use
rules.description: A document presenting a historical return series carries, where the series is used, a statement that past returns do not predict future ones.
rules.rationale: A table of past returns is read as a forecast unless something on the page says otherwise, and a qualification placed far from the table does not reach the reader at the moment they draw the inference. Placement is most of the requirement.
rules.remediation: Put the qualification at the point of use, and make the analysis behave as though it were true by varying the forward rate rather than adopting the table's mean.
rules.$assuranceNote: Lexical. It establishes that the SENTENCE is present near the series, never that it is HONOURED: "Past performance is not a guide to future returns", placed under a table and followed immediately by a projection built on that table's mean, satisfies this rule and demonstrates the exact failure it exists to prevent.

rules.title: The document states what would change its conclusion
rules.description: A document reaching a conclusion names the observation or condition that would overturn it.
rules.rationale: A conclusion with no falsifier is not an argument but a position, and it will survive every piece of contrary evidence its author later meets. Naming the falsifier in advance, before it is inconvenient, is what makes revision possible at all.
rules.remediation: State the specific observation — a rate, a threshold, an event — that would make the conclusion wrong, and where and when it would be checked.
rules.$assuranceNote: Reports NOT_EVALUATED until a person reads the conclusion and records whether a genuine falsifier was named. Whether a stated condition would actually overturn the conclusion is a judgement about the argument's structure, and an unfalsifiable sentence dressed as a falsifier — "this changes if conditions change" — is textually indistinguishable from a real one. A reviewer can see the conclusion, look for the falsifier, evaluate whether it would overturn anything, explain its absence, and remediate by stating one.
